claims.text: The proposed alloy has a density below 6 g/cm³.
The as-cast alloy has a non-equilibrium microstructure.
The initial microstructure contains a metastable solid solution.
Finely dispersed intermetallic compounds coexist with the metastable solid solution.
High-temperature exposure promotes Mg diffusion and segregation from the metastable solid solution to grain boundaries and phase interfaces.
Thermodynamic driving forces associated with the metastable state cause the proposed Mg redistribution.
Mg segregation under oxidizing exposure leads to formation of a continuous Mg-rich oxide scale at phase boundaries and interfaces.
The continuous Mg-rich oxide scale consists primarily of MgO.
The MgO-rich scale is protective and enhances passivation.
Formation of the protective scale improves oxidation resistance relative to the as-cast state.
Improved oxidation resistance will be manifested by lower mass gain.
Improved oxidation resistance will be manifested by a thinner oxide scale.
The evolved interfacial chemistry may reduce the uniform corrosion rate.
Residual intermetallic phases may produce localized corrosion effects and locally alter corrosion kinetics.
The proposed mechanism applies broadly to non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys below 6 g/cm³ in which solid solutions and stable intermetallic compounds coexist.

contradictions.description: The initial state is described as a solid solution interspersed with compositionally distinct intermetallic compounds, but the baseline is also described as having a homogeneous elemental distribution. Coexisting intermetallic phases ordinarily imply at least phase-scale elemental partitioning, so the claimed homogeneity requires qualification.

The hypothesis refers to 'observed improved oxidation resistance,' whereas the predicted-outcome field treats improved resistance as an untested prediction. No cited evidence establishes that it has already been observed.
